newsitem.title: USA: Watergate memorabilia a dud at auction.
newsitem.headline: Watergate memorabilia a dud at auction.

text.p: It may have been the political scandal of the century, but as a collector's item Watergate is a dud.
The original police report from the Watergate break-in is on sale at the Phoebus Auction Gallery in Hampton, Virginia, as is other memorabilia from the Watergate era.
Bidding on the police report reached $6,000 on Sunday, far short of the $25,000 that the anonymous owner is seeking, auctioneer Gail Wolpin told Reuters on Monday.
"The bidding process is still going on...bidding will continue over the phone," Wolpin said. "The owner wanted $25,000 at least. He would take more, actually."

The auction was timed around the 25th anniversary of the June 17, 1972, break-in at the Democratic National Committee (DNC) headquarters in Washington's Watergate Hotel, which eventually led to the only presidential resignation in U.S. history.
"(Complainant) reports office entered and several inner offices ransacked," the report says.

Other items still on the block include the ballpoint pen Nixon used to sign the SALT II treaty, Swedish crystal plates used at DNC dinners, and the form letter that President Gerald Ford sent to citizens questioning his pardon of Nixon, which exonerated the disgraced former president of any crime.
"People just bring us this stuff," auction employee Bill Welch told Reuters.
Wolpin blamed the low bidding on a local heat wave that was made worse when the Phoebus air conditioning broke down, turning the auction house into a sauna.

In any event, some members of the local Washington D.C. government are steaming, saying the original Watergate police report belongs to the city, not the rogue cop who lifted it, the Washington Post reported on Monday.
Wolpin would not confirm if the owner was a police officer, saying only that the original was left discarded on a desk at police headquarters because police rely on microfilm to file crime reports.
